title: Starter Lift-Off Credit Algorithm — scratchpad
content:
Goal: quick mental model for a starter/onramp credit that 1) gets developers to build real sessions, 2) limits exposure, and 3) gives an easy path to paid commit.

Top-level idea (Lift-Off):
- Give a small bucket of persistent credits (e.g., 10k tokens) + a time-limited session subsidy (e.g., 30 days of discounted per-session capacity).
- Credits are consumed preferentially per-session, but we amortize the expected infra cost across sessions to cap downside.
- A simple decay schedule reduces credit value after 30/60/90 days to encourage conversion.

Key heuristics and primitives (notes-to-self):
- Unit conversions: tokens <-> GPU-hour-ish. Use conservative numbers for public planning: assume 100k tokens ≈ 0.5 GPU-minutes on our baseline small LLM on dedicated infra. (ballpark; check runtime telemetry)
- SKU assumptions for starter model (v-small quant): infra cost to Redwood ≈ $0.10 per 100k tokens served (amortized across multi-tenant); margin target on starter is small but measurable.
- Risk cap per new account: want to limit max expected free cost to ~$200 over 90 days.

Example parameterization (lift-off v1):
- Persistent free bucket: 12,000 tokens (about ~12 short replies or 3 long sessions).
- Session subsidy: first 100 sessions in first 30 days get 50% off per-token charge (capped at 500 tokens/session).
- Time decay: after 30 days, persistent bucket value decays by 50%; after 90 days remaining credits expire.
- Account cap: auto-block further free-serving if estimated free-cost > $200 unless billing attached.

Back-of-envelope math (safety check):
- If our infra cost = $0.10 / 100k tokens, then 12k tokens ≈ $0.012 infra cost (negligible), but frontloaded sessions (streaming + context) can inflate cost by factors (prefix caching hit rate matters).
- Worst-case: heavy multi-turn with long context (20k tokens/session) — use session caps to prevent gaming: cap subsidy to 500 tokens/session indeed.

Design tradeoffs and why this structure: 
- Small persistent bucket = low-friction onboarding (user can try a quick end-to-end flow).
- Session subsidy promotes multi-turn testing (where product value is realized) without handing out unlimited tokens.
- Decay nudges conversion: you get some runway, then pressure to attach billing or commit.

Mechanics around token accounting (practical):
- Priority consumption: credits used first, then subsidy applied to billed tokens (i.e., subsidized tokens reduce billed tokens).
- Billing visibility: in console show projected remaining free-value in $ and tokens (assume infra cost schedule so customers can see real impact).
- Fraud heuristics: detect bulk-upload or streaming-only patterns that maximize token churn; throttle subsidy when patterns match 4+ parallel sessions > 1000 tokens each in 24h.

Conversion levers (experimentation ideas):
- Variant A: increase persistent bucket to 20k but shorten subsidy window to 14 days — hypothesis: faster product-time-to-value, faster conversion signal.
- Variant B: keep bucket small but increase per-session subsidy cap to 1k — hypothesis: more realistic chat prototypes => higher retention.
- Variant C: require CC after 50% of credits used — hypothesis: reduces fraud, improves paid conversion rate but increases friction.

Quick sensitivity table (very rough):
- Assumptions: infra cost 0.10/100k tokens. CPA target for paid conversion = $150. Conversion lift target from starter = 3%.
- If average convert from starter uses $500/year in revenue, need 0.9% conversion to justify $150 CPA. So free-cost budget per acquired starter user should be << $150 (aim for $20–$50).
- Our Lift-Off v1: persistent bucket cost ≈ $0.012, session subsidy (100 sessions * 500 tokens * 50% * infra cost) = 100 * 250 * (0.10/100k) ≈ $0.025. Combined theoretical infra cost ~ $0.04 per starter (in these conservative arithmetic). That seems tiny vs target, so dominant risk is caching/misaligned assumptions.

Operational TODOs / checks: 
- Pull actual serving telemetry: avg tokens/session for new accounts, cache hit rates, infra cost per token by model and region. (link telemetry query to compute realistic numbers)
- Build console mock: show credit burn as $ and tokens, show days remaining, show sessions subsidized.
- Add quota enforcement: session subsidy must be enforced server-side with easy rollout flags.
- A/B plan with metrics: conversion, time-to-first-paid, average tokens/month after 90 days, fraud rate.

Edge cases and notes: 
- Enterprise signups: Should bypass lift-off; instead sales-driven credits.
- Dedicated/private customers: Credits should be accounted differently (no subsidy on self-hosted infra unless negotiated).
- Partnerships: allow partner-promos to top up persistent bucket without enabling session subsidy (simpler to audit).

Open questions (for product sync):
- What is the true infra marginal cost we should assume for PRIC planning? (my placeholder 0.10/100k likely low)
- How do we instrument per-account worst-case exposure before converting? Prefer pre-compute worst-24h token churn to gate subsidies.
- Should we tie subsidy to usage patterns (e.g., only chat-style multi-turn counts) vs prompt-only bursts?

Random scribbles: 
- Consider a "lift-off badge" paired with onboarding checklist to encourage goal completion — give +5k token top-up on completing two product milestones (e.g., webhook + first user).
- Add tiny friction: require email verification + basic app description to start subsidy (helps deter bot farms).

End of scratchpad. Keep this lean; will fold into PRD after telemetry pull and 2 experiments defined.

-- Maya
